title: Go, your son lives (John 4:43–54)
hook: a royal official believes the word and walks home
tomorrow: do you want to be healed?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman ran back to town and the Samaritans came out across the fields, ripe for harvest. Your line was she left her water jar. Who did you tell, and what did you let wait? Day six hundred four.

A man with rank, and none of it helps. The King James calls him a nobleman, an official of the king, and his son is sick, at the point of death, in Capernaum. He hears Jesus is back in Galilee, at Cana, the village of the wedding. He goes up to find him. Every hour he's gone is an hour he's not at his son's bed. He finds Jesus, and he doesn't make a speech. He begs: "Sir, come down ere my child die." Come down. Come with me. Now.

Jesus's first answer sounds like a sigh, aimed at the whole crowd as much as at him: "Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe." The father doesn't argue. He just asks again. Come down before my child dies. And Jesus doesn't come. He says one short sentence, which the King James Bible gives as: "Go thy way; thy son liveth." That's all. No touch, no visit, no proof. Just a sentence, and a long road. Then John writes the line that is today's carry: "And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way." Think about that walk. He's begged for Jesus to come, and he's leaving without him, carrying nothing but a sentence. The next day, still on the road, his servants come running to meet him. Your son lives. He asks them one question: when did he start getting better? They tell him: "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The very hour Jesus said go. And John says the man believed, and his whole household with him. Notice that the word believe appears twice. First he believes the word, enough to start walking. Then, when he sees what happened, he believes in a fuller way. Here faith grows in two steps: first a step on trust, then sight. John counts this as the second sign Jesus did in Galilee, after the water turned to wine, and both happen from Cana. One at a wedding, one by a word spoken from a distance.
screen: `A LONG ROAD WITH ONLY A SENTENCE.`
then, large: `THE MAN BELIEVED THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a word on trust. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise or a word someone has given you that you can't check yet. A friend who said I'll be there. A doctor who said this will heal. A line from scripture you hold onto. Notice whether some part of you wants proof first. Then imagine taking the first step home anyway, the way the father did, with only the sentence in your pocket. If you pray, you can hold that word before God. If you don't, rest with that word a moment. The bell holds the time.
Go. Jesus's answer to a desperate father: go thy way, thy son liveth. One word that sends him home on nothing but trust.
Your line: he believed the word. Today, act on one thing someone told you in good faith, without asking for proof first. Day six hundred four.

howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this story when someone they love is ill and far away, and some churches pray for the sick by name during worship.

he never went. he said "go thy way; thy son liveth" from Cana.

fork.setup: you're the father. you begged Jesus to come with you, and he says: go, your son lives. what do you do?
options: turn around and start the long walk home.
stay in Cana until you hear news.
fork.reveal: "the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way." the good news meets him on the road.

original.note: Greek: go, be on your way. The first word of Jesus's answer in John 4:50.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus healed a sick boy by visiting him.
what it means: Jesus never went. The father walked home on a sentence, and the fever had left at that very hour.
what a scholar hears: John uses "believed" twice, first trusting the word, then believing with his household, a pattern of faith growing from trust to sight.
recall: one of the two on the road

sources.quoted: Sir, come down ere my child die.
Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.
Go thy way; thy son liveth. And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way.
Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.

notes: KJV calls him 'a certain nobleman' (4:46); Greek basilikos, a royal official, likely in Herod Antipas's service. The script names Antipas as the king; confirm.
Distance Cana–Capernaum given as about twenty miles; estimates vary with the site of Cana. Confirm.
The seventh hour taken as about 1 p.m. (counting from sunrise). Confirm.
Word is 'Go' per index; the Greek imperative in 4:50 is πορεύου. Confirm form and pronunciation.
Some scholars link this story with the centurion's servant in Matthew 8 / Luke 7; not mentioned in the script.
